objectReview.reason: Retains amorphous solids as distinct from ordinary crystals, possible neighboring-atom short-range order and absence of long-range periodic repetition by lattice translation. Does not claim amorphous means completely uncorrelated atomic positions. The last sentence is technical but explains which repetition is absent.

Retains identical chemical composition in crystalline/amorphous forms, silica and exact SiO2 notation, quartz as crystalline silica, regular hexagon network a and irregular network b with pentagons/heptagons as well as hexagons. Both are explicitly simplified local-connection/long-range-arrangement comparisons, not measurements of full three-dimensional silica crystal structure. The English does not revive the source's misleading idea of amorphous quartz.
Single original fig-81 placeholder, empty text/source_text, printed page 114 and source object order remain exact. No new geometry or duplicated display object is introduced.
Visible caption Figure 81 preserves source number and reference. Structural label and source_text remain original; caption is not counted as an English body-flow paragraph.

Retains the source isotropy topic but conditions it on uniform statistically direction-neutral structure and absence of alignment, directional fields/stress. Defines direction-independent corresponding physical properties, rather than treating every amorphous sample as universally isotropic. Retains glass, asphalt, plastics, rosin and rock sugar as source examples while explicitly correcting ordinary rock sugar to crystalline and distinguishing amorphous plastics from plastics containing crystalline regions.

Retains elasticity and time-dependent viscous response, short versus long loading times, brittle impact as conditional, sustained-load creep/flow, asphalt on a solid surface, local vibration during residence time, slower glassy structural rearrangement and solid-like response without crystal periodicity. Relates loading duration to relaxation time and preserves the explicit prohibition on inferring observable room-temperature glass flow. Does not assign every atom a common fixed residence time.

Retains low-temperature/limited-time solid-like response, heating-related faster local rearrangement, gradual softening and the absence of a single crystal-like melting point. Temperature is relative to the material's softening/glass-transition range. Glass transition is explicitly rate/time-dependent over a range and not equilibrium pure-crystal melting at specified pressure. Crystallization/decomposition and material-dependent behavior remain possible.

flowParagraphReview.reason: Introduces short-range order versus long-range periodic lattice order rather than reducing amorphous structure to total randomness.
Moves from structural distinction to same-composition states under different formation conditions; SiO2 remains exact.
Separates quartz from amorphous silica and identifies diagram a as the regular hexagonal schematic.
Identifies b and all listed polygon types, then explicitly limits both diagrams to simplified comparisons, not measured 3D structures.
Preserves every accepted isotropy condition and gives the meaning of isotropy in the next sentence. Dense wording is noted separately, not a scientific failure.
Reinforces that absent periodicity alone does not guarantee isotropy and gives noncrystallized glass as an example.
Names all remaining source examples as a textbook list, not as an unqualified modern classification.
Immediately resolves the list's two important traps: plastics can include crystal regions and ordinary rock sugar is usually crystalline.
Defines viscoelasticity from elastic and time-dependent viscous deformation, with some materials rather than all materials.
Explicitly compares loading duration with structural relaxation time and explains short-time solid-like response.
Qualifies brittle fracture and longer-time creep with material, temperature and sustained-load conditions.
Retains asphalt example while rejecting a universal observable-flow inference and specifically rejecting observable room-temperature glass flow.
Defines the textbook residence-time picture and retains nearby vibration, not immobile atoms.
Restricts slow glassy rearrangement to the timescale considered and disclaims a common fixed per-atom residence time.
Connects limited rearrangement to solid-like mechanics without conflating that with crystal periodic structure.
Uses relative low temperature and limited observation time, then explains faster rearrangement/softening with heating and a decomposition condition.
Preserves glass transition as a temperature range depending on rate/time, explicitly distinct from equilibrium melting of a pure crystal at a specified pressure.
Explains the textbook no-definite-melting-temperature statement without claiming all materials soften alike or excluding crystallization/decomposition.

readabilityNotes.note: By shifts along a crystal lattice is accurate but technical; a short explanation of a repeated pattern would ease entry for a young reader. The preceding short-/long-range contrast already preserves the meaning.

The first isotropy sentence has 33 words and several nested conditions. Splitting the direction-neutral structure, isotropy meaning and alignment/field/stress conditions into shorter sentences would improve scanning. The next sentence defines isotropy and all conditions are scientifically purposeful, so this is not a blocking loss of meaning.

The first temperature sentence also has 33 words. Equilibrium melting at specified pressure is a demanding term, but its contrast with rate/time-dependent gradual glass transition is explicitly supplied. Shorter sentences could improve accessibility without deleting conditions.
